newsitem.title: CANADA: CAW says major strides in Chrysler talks.
newsitem.headline: CAW says major strides in Chrysler talks.

text.p: Canadian Auto Workers union president Buzz Hargrove said on Monday that Chrysler Corp's Canadian unit had made major strides toward the union's position on outsourcing as the two sides worked to reach a labor agreement ahead of a Tuesday midnight strike deadline.

"We are about halfway across that giant (outsourcing) step," Hargrove told reporters during a break in bargaining. "There is an opportunity now to close out our concern on the principle of work ownership and outsourcing."
Hargrove said he was confident the outsourcing issue could be settled in the next two or three hours, which would turn the tide of the talks.

"If we can resolve this to our satisfaction in the next two or three hours, we still have time," said Hargrove. "We're confident, given the issues left, that we can do this before 1159 tomorrow night. If we don't get this issue resolved in the next two or three hours, then it's clear we have a strike on our hands."
Hargrove was slated to meet with Chrysler chief negotiator Ken Francese on the outsourcing issue at 1530 EDT/1930 GMT.
Talks on economic, work time and health and safety issues were halted Sunday, but would resume if outsourcing was settled, Hargrove said.

The union still objects to Chrysler's inclusion in the contract of a clause that allows the company to opt out of its commitment tied to work ownership, a concept Chrysler recognized in principle yesterday.

The union has said it owns work if workers produce quality products at a reasonable cost and the company is making a reasonable profit. It said owned work cannot be outsourced by the company unless it is replaced with other work.

"There still is a catch-all phrase in there that waters down that commitment really significantly," said Hargrove. "If we can get rid of this one contentious part of a sentence in the proposal, then we've nailed down this issue pretty well."
Chrysler spokesman Othmar Stein said Chrysler was "still reasonably optimistic, even though we are down to 36 hours or a little less, that we can resolve this."
He said the union's previous proposal on outsourcing was unacceptable because it limited Chrysler's ability to manage the company competitively.
"The language would simply curtail management's ability to really run a company in the most competitive fashion possible."
But Chrysler seemed to accept the need to satisfy the union on the outsourcing issue, which was identified from the outset as the union's biggest concern.

Stein said Chrysler had been reluctant to accept the union's intrusion into traditional managment rights, but he said that "by the same token, we do recognize that they do in certain instances have legitimate causes for concern."
Hargrove said Chrysler's movement on the outsourcing issue gave him renewed confidence that a strike could be averted.
"If they're willing to reach to us on this issue, there's a pretty good indication they want to do this without a strike," he said.
Hargrove has said the 2359 EDT Tuesday/0359 GMT Wednesday strike deadline would not be extended.
A collective agreement with Chrysler will become the framework for negotiations between the union and the Canadian units of General Motors Corp and Ford Motor Co.
